readings.author: Ruth Wedgwood
readings.title: Unilateral Action in a Multilateral World
readings.summary:
From *Multilateralism and U.S. Foreign Policy* (2001).
- **Web of institutions**: environment, human rights, children, trade, IP, the spectrum, capital markets (informal discipline); NATO, OSCE, OAS; ad hoc groups (Contadora, 'contact groups', 'Friends of the Secretary-General'). Informality can help (COCOM, the Australia Group, the nuclear suppliers group, KEDO).
- **Why multilateralism**: coordination; binding potential spoilers; economies of scale; preventing free-riding; legitimacy (values not one country's interest); credibility of regimes.
- **Its problems**: slowness, generality masking differences, rivalries, monitoring and defection, unstable coalitions, secrecy, uneven bureaucracies, cultural misunderstanding, interoperability.
- **Force multilaterally**: joint commitments restrain arms races (NATO and Germany; US troops in Korea and Japan; 'virtual' nuclear states). Security Council or art. 51 authorisation gives legitimacy, mobilises democratic support and basing, and can police conduct (Desert Storm stopped short of Baghdad). But the UN never got art. 43 forces; it is a 'legal umbrella and political sounding board', authorising member states (Korea 1950, Gulf 1991 under US command). Alliances also manage domestic politics (Res. 678 and Congress).
- **Conclusion**: Security Council delays push the US to 'substitute' multilateralism (regional organisations, coalitions), plus consultation and public argument, which 'may cause sleepless nights for some international lawyers'. The US won't let multilateral machinery govern its force, because deterrence requires adversaries to know a response will come; otherwise blocking mechanisms could cause conflict. 'Creative ambiguity' continues.
arguments: Multilateralism is valuable but instrumentally so.
UN collective security never materialised as designed.
'Substitute multilateralism' as legitimacy without Council authorisation.
Unilateral options preserve deterrence.
readings.tldr: The US built a dense web of multilateral institutions, which coordinate, share costs, prevent free-riding and confer legitimacy. But multilateral bodies are slow, vague, hard to monitor, and the UN never worked as designed (no art. 43 forces). On force, the US often uses 'substitute multilateralism' (regional bodies, ad hoc coalitions) and keeps unilateral options, because deterrence needs credibility that a blocking veto would undermine: 'creative ambiguity'.
readings.context: A Yale/US-policy voice in 'Managing an Empire'. It sets up [[slaughter-around-un]] (2003), contrasts with [[nicaragua-1984]] (judicial control of force) and connects to Topic 22.

readings.author: Anne-Marie Slaughter
readings.title: Good Reasons for Going Around the U.N.
readings.tldr: On the eve of the 2003 Iraq invasion: giving up on the Security Council is 'illegal but legitimate', like Kosovo 1999. UN approval may come after the fact if WMD are found or Iraqis welcome the intervention and the UN is brought back to rebuild. What matters is that all sides still treat UN approval as necessary; the rules may have to evolve so that what is legitimate is also legal.
readings.summary:
NYT op-ed, 18 March 2003.
- **Kosovo precedent**: in 1999 NATO bypassed an expected Russian veto; the Independent International Commission found the intervention 'formally illegal' but 'legitimate'.
- **Iraq**: UN approval could come *after* an invasion if WMD are found, or even without them if Iraqis welcome the coalition and the US returns to the UN to rebuild. The US will claim authorisation under Res. 1441; most international lawyers will reject that; insisting on formal legality 'may be counterproductive'.
- Neither side can command a veto-free majority; both continue to claim the better argument. Importantly, everyone still treats UN approval as necessary (compare the Cold War Council sidelined, or a US invasion without any UN reference).
- The UN constrains decision-making but 'cannot be a straitjacket' on self-defence or vital security interests. Its founders built a political as well as a legal institution, wary of the 'best' being the 'enemy of the good'.
- An 'unruly process of pushing and shoving' redefines the UN's role without amendment (East Timor showed consensus is possible). 'The rules may have to evolve, so that what is legitimate is also legal.'
arguments: 'Illegal but legitimate' as a category.
Legitimacy can be retroactive and outcome-based.
UN centrality preserved as a reference point even when bypassed.
Practice changes the rules without formal amendment.
readings.context: The liberal-internationalist case for flexible legality. Compare [[wedgwood-unilateral]] (substitute multilateralism), [[koskenniemi-impunity]] (law and politics), Krever's warning about legalism ([[krever-scurrying]], Iraq 2003), and Topic 22 ([[kennedy-legal-expertise-war]]).

readings.sub: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
readings.author: Louis Henkin
readings.title: How Nations Behave: Law and Foreign Policy
readings.tldr: To many observers international law seems voluntary and hortatory, yielding to national interest. Lawyers answer that the cup is half full: law is made and grows, there is a Court, arbitration, national courts and UN organs, and horizontal enforcement. Above all, critics ask the wrong questions. What matters is whether law is *observed* and shapes behaviour, and it largely is.
readings.summary:
From *How Nations Behave* (2nd ed. 1979), pp. 25–26.
- **The sceptic's view**: governments seem free to agree to new law, to accept others' views, and to comply or not. International law is 'voluntary and only hortatory' and must yield to national interest (security, power, prestige). Diplomats think it unrealistic to build policy on it and are impatient with their lawyers.
- **Lawyers' reply**: admit the limits but deny their implications; reject Austin's definition; law grows even if slowly; the ICJ's few judgments are respected; arbitration fills gaps; national courts develop the law; Security Council and General Assembly actions interpret and develop law and deter; there is 'horizontal enforcement' by other nations' reactions.
- **The right question**: not whether there are legislative, judicial and executive branches like a domestic system, but 'whether international law is reflected in the policies of nations'. Not whether law is enforced but 'whether law is observed, whether it governs or influences behavior'. 'Nations have accepted important limitations on their sovereignty', observed them, and the result is 'substantial order'.
- *(The famous line, 'almost all nations observe almost all principles of international law and almost all of their obligations almost all of the time', comes later in the book and is not in this excerpt.)*
arguments: Shift from enforcement to compliance as the test of law.
Institutional gaps are partly filled by other mechanisms.
Observance, not structure, makes international law real.
readings.context: 'Back to norms and values' after the policy-science moment ([[mcdougal-law-power]]); answers [[austin-province]] differently from [[kelsen-lecture-iii]] (behaviour, not sanction). Koh builds on it ([[koh-tlp]]).

readings.sub: Moment 3 – Back to Norms and Values?
readings.author: Louis Henkin
readings.title: International Law and the Inter-State System
readings.summary:
From *International Law: Politics and Values* (1995), Part I.
- Any legal system reflects its political system; international law reflects an inter-state system.
- *Law is politics*: the law/politics distinction is 'only a part-truth'. Law is the resultant of political forces, and its influence on behaviour is politically determined. But law isn't depreciated: it 'permeates, supports and maintains' the system and shapes how nations behave; lawyers, courts, publicists and bodies like the Institut and the ALI enrich or impoverish it.
- Domestic law expresses a domestic society of people (and juristic persons) and serves order, reliable expectations, protection of persons and property, welfare and justice.
- International law analogously serves order, expectations, protection of 'persons' and values, but its constituency is *states*: an inter-state system.
arguments: Law and politics are intertwined, not opposed.
International law mirrors a state-centred political system.
The domestic analogy is useful with caution.
readings.tldr: 'Law is politics': made by political actors, through political procedures, for political ends. But law also permeates and shapes the political system. International law is the normative expression of an *inter-state* system whose 'persons' are states, not human beings, with purposes (order, reliable expectations, protection, values) analogous to domestic law.
readings.context: Mainstream liberal statism in 1995, the counterpoint to Jessup's transnationalism ([[jessup-transnational]]) and Kennedy's critique of the state-centred frame. Compare Álvarez ('pure law does not exist', [[corfu-1949-merits]]) and McDougal ([[mcdougal-law-power]]).

concepts.short: Unwritten law from general state practice plus opinio juris (acceptance as law).

Sovereigntist rejection vs. structural critique of international criminal justice.
From bilateral countermeasures to economic warfare by sanctions.
A linear progress story (natural law → positivism → institutions) vs. a grid of shifting professional sensibilities driven by traumas.
The casebook's 'League era' becomes a Modernist cultural project with its own blind spots, not merely a failed step toward the UN.
Berman uses Redslob as a key example of legal Modernism: nationalism as a 'crater' law must both follow and discipline.
Fills in the 1900–1950 row: minority rights, self-determination, the jurist as hero.
The intro previews Austin's view of international law as 'positive morality', taken up in Topic 12.
The doctrine of sources promised a positive science of law; Schachter shows its inductive method is partly myth.
The ILC conclusions try to answer the casebook's open questions about practice, opinio juris, treaties and resolutions.
Conflicting practice (deterrence vs non-use) and contested opinio juris leave custom undecidable.
Paquete finds a custom of *restraint* from practice and humanity; Lotus refuses to infer a restraining custom from abstention.
Lotus: freedom unless prohibited by consent. McDougal: claims are accepted or rejected by reasonableness in an ongoing process.
Shows that Art. 38(1)(c)'s 'general principles' covers five different foundations, ultimately resting on consensus.
Both trace a natural-law current inside positive law; jus cogens turns it into strict hierarchy.
Same feminist project across Topics 3–4: from the gender of peremptory norms to the gender of sovereignty.
A court cautiously preserving treaty rights in war vs. an executive declaring a treaty suspended for policy.
The ICJ applied the narrow VCLT tests and rejected Hungary's changed-circumstances and impossibility claims.
Two nuclear cases where the Court avoids ruling on legality: mootness in 1974, non liquet in 1996.
The imputability rules of state responsibility leave out states that tolerate endemic private violence against women.
Montevideo's dry criteria were a semi-peripheral victory: civilisation dropped, recognition made declaratory, non-intervention won.

Álvarez brings his interwar 'new international law' into an ICJ opinion.
Divisible sovereignty returns as the feminist and pluralist idea of overlapping, layered sovereignties.
Policy-science disaggregates sovereignty and invites participation but rests on liberal, rationalist assumptions.
Formally independent small states live in 'constrained sovereignty' under dyadic, imperial constitutions.
Statehood contested through historical narrative as a prelude to invasion.
Recognition beyond states: a platform 'recognises' Indigenous peoples while the state withholds constitutional recognition.

Both build from exclusive territorial sovereignty and consent as the source of any limit.

Nicaragua quotes Tehran: the Court won't decline the legal aspect of a dispute because it has political ones, or because the Security Council is seized.
The Court cites Corfu Channel to show it has never shied from cases involving use of force.
Both make legal status track social fact: effective government, effective nationality.
A formal, investor-limiting rule between Western states vs. the later investment arbitration regime critiqued for bias against the Third World.
Iran's anti-imperial framing (1953 coup, exploitation) is the kind of history the NIEO and TWAIL put at the centre, but the Court sets it aside.
Nationality is set domestically but limited internationally when invoked against other states.
Feminists won recognition of sexual violence as a grave international crime, but the criminal-law frame narrowed the wider feminist agenda.
From scepticism about trials' truth-telling to a TWAIL/Marxist warning against juridifying resistance.
Law's individualising, narrow frame can't capture the many causes and the broader meaning of atrocity.
The fight over context (sudden vs long vs slow violence) applied to 7 October and Gaza.
Miller's earlier critique of Oslo's 'permanent transition' underpins the 'infinite present' of occupation.
Both examine the gap between the legal and the discursive meaning of genocide in Gaza.
A pattern of US exit from international adjudication when its use of force is at stake.
Nuremberg's 'crimes are committed by men, not abstract entities' is the premise Koskenniemi questions.
The Restatement's bases and 'reasonableness' factors all run through an indeterminate 'national interest' that hides normative choices.
From exposing national-interest talk to a positive cosmopolitan pluralist theory of jurisdiction and community.
Comity balancing applied by the forum court, and resolved for the forum.
From subpoenaing offshore bank records to secondary sanctions that make dollar-linked firms worldwide comply.
Secondary sanctions as precursors to the sanctions-as-economic-battlefield moment.
The Pinochet saga: Spain's assertion of jurisdiction and the House of Lords' denial of immunity for torture.

Self-determination as a limit on any transfer of territory.

Sanctions on Russia strain the line between countermeasures, retorsion and economic warfare.
Takes Vitoria's logic (Indian personality granted in order to be bound) into 19th-century positivism and treaties of cession.
Both read Lawrence: 'civilization' as an indefinable but decisive legal category that constructs Europe against non-Europe.

Westlake's view, 'of the uncivilized natives international law takes no account', underlies title contests between empires.
'General principles recognized by civilized nations' is the colonial vocabulary surviving in the canonical source list.

Divisible sovereignty and protectorates: control without the burden of formal sovereignty, calibrated to imperial interests.

Personal and regional autonomy as early versions of layered, non-territorial sovereignty.
Natural frontiers and state integrity vs the decolonial choice of frozen administrative lines.
Berman's 'pragmatist/functionalist' lawyer, dividing tasks to minimise conflict, descends from Jessup's functional approach.
Two critiques of 19th-century international law between the wars: Álvarez's solidarist reconstruction vs Nazi Volk and Grossraum theory.
Kelsen: decentralised sanctions (reprisals, war) make international law a coercive order, so Austin's 'no sovereign, no law' fails.
McDougal rejects law as norms-and-sanctions for law as authoritative decision within the world power process.

Álvarez's solidarist 'new international law' and judicial law-making vs Kelsen's pure, positivist account of validity.

Transnational law of many actors vs an inter-state system whose 'persons' are states.
From 'substitute multilateralism' to 'illegal but legitimate' (Kosovo, Iraq).
Law as policy and world-order building, the 1950–89 row's 'functional problem solving'.

themes.name: Sovereignty: absolute, divided, relative
themes.description: Follow how sovereignty is asserted, divided, limited and re-asserted across the course.

themes.name: Where does law end?
themes.description: Custom, twilight agreements, declarations, Austin vs Kelsen, WTO 'less is more': the course keeps returning to the boundary of law.

themes.name: Empire, colonialism and hierarchy
themes.description: Who was inside and outside the 'family of nations', and how that shaped the law's basic categories.

themes.name: Law and the global economy
themes.description: Property as sovereignty, ordoliberal design, WTO, value chains, sanctions: law distributes economic power.

themes.name: Feminist critique
themes.description: The gendered public/private divide, from jus cogens to sovereignty to the language of war.

themes.name: People with projects: expertise and its dark sides
themes.description: Kennedy's through-line: international law as professional practice, with costs that its practitioners don't see.

themes.name: Fact vs form: effectiveness against legal title
themes.description: Again and again the cases choose between what is *actually* the case (effective control, real connection) and what the *paper* says (recognition, title, incorporation). Notice which way each case goes, and who benefits.

themes.name: Who decides? Courts, political organs and self-help
themes.description: In a system without a central enforcer, who gets the last word: the ICJ, the Security Council, a national court, or the injured state acting alone? Track how each forum claims or avoids authority.
